memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then Joseph directed the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel. So the physicians embalmed him, taking a full forty days, for that was the time required for embalming. And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days." — Gen 50:2-3 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Seventy days of mourning. All Egypt joins in — an entire nation grieving a foreign shepherd, because of who his son was.

Notice the length of it. Forty days for the embalming, seventy days of national mourning. Nobody was in a hurry. Their culture built time into loss and did not expect people to be functioning again by the following week.

We have largely lost this. Modern life gives grief a few days and then expects normal service to resume. People return to work with a hole in their lives and are quietly expected to have processed it.

Scripture does not work that way. Israel mourned Moses for thirty days (Deut 34:8). Job's friends sat with him in silence for seven days before anyone said a word — and that was the wisest thing they ever did (Job 2:13).

If you are grieving, give yourself time. If you know someone who is, do not measure their sorrow against your schedule. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15).

Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is simply be present, without fixing anything.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have you rushed your own grief or someone else's?
2. Who could you simply sit with this week, without trying to fix anything?
3. What does it say about God that He allows time for sorrow?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, teach me to give grief the time it needs, in myself and in others. Help me be present with people in their sorrow rather than hurrying them through it. Amen.
